Commentary on Surat al-Ghashiya

It is Meccan by consensus.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?﴾ That is: the Resurrection. It is called "the Overwhelming" because it overwhelms everything with its terrors. It is also said: it overwhelms every disbeliever and wrongdoer with punishment. Al-ghashiya is also al-mujallala (the one that covers all over). The meaning of "Has there come to you" is: "Indeed there has come to you."

Qur'an 88:2 is quoted as: ﴿Faces, that Day, will be downcast﴾.

And His saying: ﴿Faces, that Day, downcast﴾ means: humbled, abased, because of what they see of the evil end. The meaning is that abasement has overtaken them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 88, verse 3:

And His saying: ﴿Labouring, weary﴾ means: they worked in this world for other than God, so they became weary and exhausted in the Hereafter through the punishment of God.

It is related from al-Suddi and a group (of scholars) that they are the monks and the people of the monasteries among the Christians and the Jews.

It has also been narrated from ʿUmar that when he came to al-Sham, he passed by the cell of a monk and called out to him. The monk looked down at him, and he had become emaciated from hunger, hardship and worship, and he was wearing a burnous. ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, wept. They said, "O Commander of the Faithful, what makes you weep?" He said, "A poor man who sought a matter and did not attain it, and took a path and went astray from it." Then he recited His saying: ﴿Labouring, weary﴾, and the verse.
"And His saying: ﴿They will burn in a scorching fire﴾, meaning: they will endure its heat."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 88, verse 5:

And His saying: ﴿They will be given drink from a boiling spring﴾, meaning: it has reached the utmost of heat.

Al-Hasan al-Basri (ḥasan al-Baṣrī) said: Jahannam has been kindled beneath it since it was created, so they are brought to it as a thirsty herd, i.e., parched with thirst.

The poet al-Nabigha (al-Nābigha) said:

(He dyes his mane, (having betrayed), and it is humiliated ... with a red [liquid] from the entire belly, boiling)

In some tafsirs: when they approach it, it strips the skin from their faces, and when they drink from it, it cuts their intestines.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 88, verse 6:

As for His saying: ﴿There is no food for them except from ḍarī'﴾, it is a tree called in the Ḥijāz al-shibraq (a thorny plant), which has many thorns; when it dries out it is called ḍarī' (dry, thorny herb).

Ibn Qutaybah said: ḍarī' is a thing which, if camels graze on it, they perish from emaciation.

It is also said: ḍarī' is stones, and this is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others, but it is a rare opinion (qawl gharīb).

It is also said: it is a plant in which there is poison.

In the tafsir (narrations) it is reported that Allah imposed hunger upon the people of the Fire until it equals the punishment they are in. So they cry out for help and are given ḍarī' to eat. Then they cry out again and are given food that chokes (ṭa'ām dhū ghuṣṣah). Then they recall that in the world they used to ward off choking with water, so they cry out for help, and they are left for a thousand years asking for water, and then they are given boiling water (al-ḥamīm) to drink.

Wa-qawluhu: ﴿Neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger.﴾ It is related that the polytheists said: "Our camels grow fat on ḍarīʿ (a thorny, bitter plant of the Hijaz)." They lied in this claim, so God Most High revealed: ﴿Neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger.﴾
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Some faces on that Day will be pleasant﴾, meaning: possessors of blessing (dhāt niʿma).
And His saying: ﴿Pleased with their striving﴾, that is: well-pleasing (mardiyyah).

In the Lord's words, ﴿In a lofty Garden, where they will hear no idle talk﴾: "lāghiyah" means "laghw" (idle talk), the feminine form used as a verbal noun, and it is

in the sense of His words: ﴿where they will hear no idle talk or sinful speech﴾.

"And His saying: ﴿Therein is a flowing spring﴾ — we have already explained it before."

"And His saying: ﴿Therein are couches raised high﴾, meaning: elevated above the ground of Paradise.

It is also said in the tafsir: the couches are raised high, and upon them are stuffed cushions, each cushion like a dome (junbudh).

And it is also related in it that they lower themselves for the believer, so that when he climbs onto them, they rise up."
And His saying: ﴿And cups set in place﴾. We have already explained the meaning of al-akwab (cups), which are the pitchers that have no spouts.

And His saying: ﴿And cushions arranged in rows﴾ — meaning: cushions placed in rows, one beside another. The poet said:

(Indeed we pass the cup around among our drinking companions, and between us and Abu Qabus, upon the cushions.)

And His saying: ﴿And carpets spread out﴾ — that is, rugs (bisaṭ); its singular is zarbiyya.

And His saying: ﴿spread out﴾ — scattered about; the meaning of "scattered" is that they have been distributed throughout the gatherings, and the gatherings have been furnished with them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 88, verse 17:

And the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Will they not look?﴾ If it is said: how does this fit with what came before?

The answer: when the Prophet mentioned to them what Allah had promised the disbelievers and what He had promised the believers, they found this extremely hard to accept.

They said: "We do not understand life after death, and we do not know of any promise or any threat." So Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse, and mentioned to them the proofs that lie within the range of their sight.

Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi, may Allah be pleased with them, said: Allah, the Exalted, mentioned these four: the camels, the sky, the earth, and the mountains, and singled them out from among all other things, because the Bedouin, when he mounts his camel and goes out into the desert, sees nothing but the camel he is riding, the sky above him, the earth beneath him, and the mountains that are right before his eyes.

As for His saying: ﴿At the camel, how it is created?﴾, there is in the camel a wonder of creation that is not found in any other animal, because it, despite its size and bulk, submits to whoever leads it. Also, it kneels down so that a heavy load can be placed upon it, and it rises up from its kneeling, and this is not found in any other animal. A small child can lead it and it submits, and he can make it kneel and it kneels.

In some accounts it is related that a mouse ran off with the halter of a camel and entered its burrow, so the camel lay down, and the mouse dragged the halter until the camel's mouth was placed at the entrance of the hole.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 88, verses 18–20:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And at the sky, how it was raised; and at the mountains, how they were set up; and at the earth, how it was spread out﴾. That is: spread out (busitat).

It is reported from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' that His words ﴿at the camels, how they were created﴾ refer to the clouds. This is an anomalous (shadh) opinion. It is permissible to take this reading as the basis for that one when the word is read with shadda (tashdid) and with a long vowel (madd).

It has been read, in the anomalous (shadh) reading, with tashdid.

Al-Mubarrad said: It has been said that al-ibil means the large pieces of cloud. It is said: so-and-so yuwabbil over so-and-so, meaning he magnifies and exalts himself over him.

Almost. Translation:

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So remind; you are only one who reminds﴾. In the exegesis: it is an admonition for the believer and a proof against the disbeliever. And it is said: "Remind" means: recall the proofs of the Oneness of Allah, the Exalted, and the blessings He has bestowed upon him.

Wa-qawluhu: ﴿You are not over them a controller.﴾ That is, not a dominator (musallat). And it has been said: this was before the verse of the sword; but after its revelation, he was given authority over them.

The passage's wording: "وَقَوله: ﴿إِلَّا من تولى وَكفر﴾ اسْتثِْنَاء مُنْقَطع كَأَنَّهُ قَالَ: لَكِن من تولى وَكفر ﴿فيعذبه الله الْعَذَاب الْأَكْبَر﴾".

Translation:

And His saying: ﴿Except for one who turns away and disbelieves﴾ is an exceptive clause that is disjunct (munqati', i.e., the exception is not of the same kind as what precedes it), as if He had said: "But whoever turns away and disbelieves," ﴿then Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment﴾.

And His saying: ﴿Except for one who turns away and disbelieves﴾ is an exceptive clause that is disjunct (munqati', i.e., the exception is not of the same kind as what precedes it), as if He had said: "But whoever turns away and disbelieves," ﴿then Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment﴾.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾ — meaning, their going back. It is said: "āba yaʾūbu" (he returned) when he came back. The poet said:

(Every absent one returns, / but the absent one of death does not return.)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 88, verse 26:

And His saying: "Then indeed upon Us is their reckoning" (thumma inna 'alayna hisabahum), i.e., on the Day of Resurrection.

If it is said: He said, "They have no food except from ḍarī' (a thorny plant)" [88:6], and He said in another place, "So there is not for him this Day any close friend here, nor any food except from ghislīn (the pus of the people of Hell)" [69:35–36]. So how is the reconciliation between them?

The answer has several aspects. First: ḍarī' and ghislīn are one and the same.

The second aspect: this is for one group, and that is for another group.

The third aspect: ghislīn is a food that does not benefit and does not suffice them from anything, so ḍarī' was placed in the position of that, since the two have one meaning. This was mentioned by al-Naḥḥās. And Allah knows best.
